extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (real analysis / advanced calculus); instructors and learners working through exercises on the Riemann integral
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter section giving definitions, theorems, examples and exercises about the Riemann integral: integrability criteria, properties of integrals, the fundamental theorem(s) of calculus, substitution, logarithm/exponential via integrals, and improper integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: First form of the fundamental theorem of calculus (Theorem 5.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let F be such that F' = f on (a,b) and f is continuous on [a,b]. Then for x in (a,b) we have f(x) = F'(x) and ∫_a^b f = F(b) − F(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea uses partitions and the mean value theorem on subintervals: area of i-th rectangle = f(c_i)Δx_i = F(x_i) − F(x_{i−1}), sum telescopes to F(b) − F(a). The text remarks a finite number of nondifferentiable points of F is allowable (left as an exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second form of the fundamental theorem of calculus (Theorem 5.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:[a,b]→ℝ is Riemann integrable and define F(x)=∫_a^x f, then F is continuous on [a,b]. Moreover, if f is continuous at c then F is differentiable at c and F'(c)=f(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: f bounded ⇒ F is Lipschitz (use an M bound). For differentiability at c use ε–δ: continuity of f at c gives bounds f(c)±ε on a small interval, then divide integrals by x−c and let x→c to get F'(c)=f(c). Remark: if f is continuous on [a,b] then F' = f everywhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of variables (u-substitution) theorem (Theorem 5.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let g:[a,b]→[c,d] be continuously differentiable, let f:[c,d]→ℝ be continuous, and suppose g([a,b]) ⊂ [c,d]. Then ∫_a^b f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(s) ds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: Define F(y)=∫_y^c f and use the second form of the fundamental theorem together with the chain rule: (F◦g)' = F'(g) g' = f(g) g'. The text warns to verify hypotheses (continuity, differentiability) before applying u-substitution and gives an incorrect-example caution (Example 5.3.7 involving ln|x|).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of improper integral as limit (Definition 5.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Riemann integrable on every [a,c] for c<b, define ∫_a^b f := lim_{c→b^-} ∫_a^c f if the limit exists. Similarly for infinite endpoints: ∫_a^∞ f := lim_{c→∞} ∫_a^c f, provided the limit exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the limit exists the improper integral converges; otherwise it diverges. For finite endpoints and bounded f this recovers the usual integral; for unbounded functions or unbounded intervals this provides the extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: p-test for integrals (Proposition 5.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The improper integral ∫_1^∞ 1/x^p dx converges if and only if p>1 (it converges to 1/(p−1) when p>1). The improper integral ∫_0^1 1/x^p dx converges if and only if p<1 (and diverges if p≥1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the fundamental theorem (antiderivative x^{1−p}/(1−p)) and taking limits; handle p=1 separately. This is the standard test used to compare tail behavior of integrands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison test for improper integrals (Proposition 5.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f,g be Riemann integrable on [a,b] for all b>a, and suppose 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x≥a. (i) If ∫_a^∞ g converges then ∫_a^∞ f converges. (ii) If ∫_a^∞ f diverges then ∫_a^∞ g diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses inequalities on partial integrals: for b<c, ∫_b^c g ≥ ∫_b^c f, and taking limits/the tail test shows convergence or divergence accordingly. Use nonnegativity assumption for direct comparison; the exercises/remarks note that variants exist for other improper limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail decomposition / equivalence for improper integrals (Proposition 5.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be Riemann integrable on every [a,b] for b>a. Then ∫_a^∞ f converges iff for some b>a the tail integral ∫_b^∞ f converges; when it converges one has ∫_a^∞ f = ∫_a^b f + ∫_b^∞ f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses splitting integrals at c>b and letting c→∞. This is useful to reduce convergence questions to tails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonnegative integrand supremum identity and sequence criterion (Proposition 5.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:[a,∞)→ℝ is nonnegative and Riemann integrable on every [a,b], then (i) ∫_a^∞ f = sup_{x≥a} ∫_a^x f (this supremum may be ∞). (ii) If x_n→∞ then ∫_a^∞ f converges iff the sequence ∫_a^{x_n} f has a finite limit (and the two limits agree).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: monotonicity of the function x↦∫_a^x f, Cauchy-sequence/tail control for sequences; allows checking convergence along convenient sequences (tails).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone functions are Riemann integrable (Exercise 5.2.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:[a,b]→ℝ is increasing (or decreasing) then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use a uniform partition; each subinterval has the same length so upper and lower sums approach each other as the mesh goes to zero. Part (c) uses this to show differences of increasing functions are integrable (h = f − g where f,g increasing ⇒ h integrable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step functions and elementary step functions are integrable (Exercises 5.2.12–5.2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: An elementary step function φ_I which equals 1 on I and 0 off I (I a bounded interval) is integrable on [a,b]; more generally, a finite linear combination of such φ_{I_k} (a step function) is integrable and its integral equals the sum α_k times the measure (length) of I_k (adjusted to [a,b]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise asks to consider all types of intervals (closed, open, half-open) and compute the integral in terms of endpoints. Use only the definition of the integral (upper/lower sums).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded function with finitely many discontinuities is Riemann integrable
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is bounded on [a,b] and has only finitely many discontinuities then f is Riemann integrable on [a,b] (this fact is referenced in exercises and corollaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Exercise 5.2.11 and elsewhere; typical proof: exclude small neighborhoods around finitely many discontinuities to make upper−lower sum difference small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thomae (popcorn) function is Riemann integrable (Exercise 5.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Thomae function (f(x)=1/k for rational x=m/k in lowest terms, and f(x)=0 for irrational x) is Riemann integrable on [0,1] and ∫_0^1 f = 0, despite being discontinuous on a dense set (the rationals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise is labeled 'Hard' and demonstrates that discontinuity on a dense set does not preclude Riemann integrability; proof uses that rationals with small denominators are scarce and can be enclosed in short intervals to make upper sums small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean value theorem for integrals (Exercise 5.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:[a,b]→ℝ is continuous, then there exists c∈(a,b) such that ∫_a^b f = f(c)(b−a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard consequence of continuity and the intermediate value theorem applied to the continuous function averaged over the interval; the text lists it as an exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonnegative continuous function with zero integral is identically zero (Exercise 5.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:[a,b]→ℝ is continuous and f(x)≥0 for all x and ∫_a^b f = 0, then f(x)=0 for all x in [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Exercise 5.2.6; proof uses continuity: if f(x0)>0 then by continuity there's a small interval where f>0 producing positive integral contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity and monotonicity of the integral (exercises and text)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are integrable on [a,b] then f+g and scalar multiples are integrable and ∫(f+g)=∫f+∫g, ∫(cf)=c∫f. Also if f≤g pointwise then ∫f ≤ ∫g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises (e.g., parts of 5.2.16) ask to show inequalities and provide examples where inequalities are strict when functions are not integrable; use properties of upper and lower sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration by parts (Exercise 5.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F and G are continuously differentiable on [a,b], then ∫_a^b G' F(x) dx = F(b)G(b) − F(a)G(a) − ∫_a^b F' G(x) dx (equivalently, ∫ F G' = FG|_a^b − ∫ F' G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise asks to prove the formula using the fundamental theorem of calculus and product rule; hypotheses require continuous differentiability on [a,b].

rubrics_metrics.name: Function defined by integral is Lipschitz when integrand bounded (from Theorem 5.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is bounded on [a,b] (|f|≤M) then F(x)=∫_a^x f is Lipschitz with Lipschitz constant M, hence continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses |F(x)−F(y)| ≤ M|x−y| for x,y in [a,b]. This is used to show continuity of the integral-primitive even when f is merely integrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Lebesgue style lemma (Exercise 5.2.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:[a,b]→ℝ is continuous and define x_n = ∫_a^b f(t) sin(nt) dt, then lim_{n→∞} x_n = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise asks to prove a version of the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma for continuous integrands with oscillatory factors sin(nt); standard proof uses integration by parts or equidistribution/orthogonality ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties and construction of the natural logarithm via integral (Proposition 5.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define L(x)=∫_1^x (1/t) dt for x>0. Then L(1)=0, L'(x)=1/x, L is strictly increasing, bijective onto ℝ, L(xy)=L(x)+L(y), and for rational q, L(x^q)=q L(x). Limits: lim_{x→0+} L(x)=−∞ and lim_{x→∞} L(x)=∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses second FTC, change of variables for multiplicativity, and intermediate value/Archimedean properties to show onto-ness. This motivates defining ln(x)=L(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties and construction of exponential as inverse of logarithm (Proposition 5.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define E as inverse of L (ln). Then E(0)=1, E'(x)=E(x), E is strictly increasing and maps ℝ→(0,∞), E(x+y)=E(x)E(y), and for rational q, E(qx)=E(x)^q. Define exp(x)=E(x) and e=exp(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties follow from inverse-function theorem and properties of L. The text notes E is unique with these properties and that exponentiation x^y for arbitrary real y is defined by exp(y ln x) for x>0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions about substitution and domain hypotheses (Example 5.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: One must check the hypotheses (continuity, differentiability and domain) before applying substitution: the text gives an incorrect 'solution' attempt using g(x)=ln|x| on [−1,1] which fails because ln|x| is undefined at 0, unbounded, not continuous on the interval, hence not Riemann integrable there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example emphasizes verifying that the composite and derivative are continuous (or at least integrable) on the interval in question before using change-of-variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating comparison and tail tests for convergence of improper integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete example: ∫_1^∞ sin(x^2) x^3/(x+1)(x+2) dx converges because for x≥1 the integrand is bounded by 3/x^2 and ∫_1^∞ 1/x^2 converges; hence by comparison and tail tests the original integral converges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text demonstrates typical strategy: bound complicated integrand by a p-test-friendly function for large x, then apply comparison/tail propositions.
